title: MY SON TOLD ME I WAS TOO OLD TO ATTEND HIS WEDDING (PART 2) – Story Loom

author: admin

blocks.text: …mother. He told me his ‘real mom’ is Diane. Your ex-husband’s wife. He said you were the one who walked out on him.”
I sat down at my kitchen table very slowly.

My ex-husband, Greg, left when our son, Ryan, was four. He left a note on the refrigerator and drove to Arizona with a woman from his office. I didn’t hear from him for twenty years. No child support. No birthday cards. Nothing. I raised Ryan on two jobs and a lot of prayer.

Three years ago, Greg reappeared. He’d made money in real estate. He was remarried to that same woman, Diane. He reached out to Ryan on Facebook. Ryan told me, and I told him he was an adult and could decide for himself. I didn’t know what Greg had told him.

“Ryan said his father told him everything,” his fiancée, Emma, said softly. “That you’d kicked Greg out. That you’d kept Ryan from him. That you’d hidden twenty years of letters. Ryan believes it. Greg and Diane have been paying for half our wedding. Ryan wanted them in the front row. He was afraid you’d make a scene.”
I didn’t say anything for a long time. Then I went to my closet and took out a shoebox I’d kept for thirty years.

Inside was the note Greg had left on the refrigerator. “I’m not cut out for this. Don’t look for me.” Court papers from my attempts to collect child support, all returned undeliverable. And a stack of letters. From me to Greg. Every year on Ryan’s birthday, for ten years. Begging him to call his son. All of them stamped “Return to Sender.”
I mailed copies to Emma. She gave them to Ryan.
He called me three days later, at midnight. He didn’t say hello. He said, “Mom, I’m so sorry.”
He’d confronted his father. Greg had admitted everything. He’d been ashamed of abandoning his son. When he came back, it was easier to tell Ryan a story where he was the victim.
“I believed him over you,” Ryan said. “You. The person who raised me alone. I’m so ashamed.”
“You wanted a father,” I said. “That’s not something to be ashamed of.”
Ryan told Greg and Diane they were no longer invited to the wedding. He paid them back for their half, with money he and Emma had saved for a house. I reinstated every payment I’d canceled.

At the wedding, Ryan walked me down the aisle to my seat in the front row. Then, before the ceremony started, he took the microphone and said, “I want to thank my mom. She’s the only parent who ever showed up. Every single day. I almost forgot that. I never will again.”
I’m sixty-nine. I danced until midnight. I didn’t embarrass anyone. Except maybe Ryan, a little, during the Electric Slide.
